name: Hydrolyzed keratin

lead: Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin, from sources such as feathers or wool, cut into small fragments so it dissolves in water. It is added to conditioners and masks to strengthen and smooth damaged hair for a healthier, shinier look.

Proponents say the small protein fragments deposit on or fill gaps in damaged hair. A 120-person trial of a keratin peptide powder for hair health is registered as completed with no results posted; most other published work is on non-cosmetic biomaterials.

paras: It is used in conditioners, masks and repair treatments, with the smoothing effect felt after application and often maintained through regular use.
No hair-specific safety findings are described in the sources reviewed. It is an ordinary cosmetic ingredient, and products vary.

trials.title: Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Hydrolyzed Keratin Peptide Powder on Hair Health

angle.text: Hydrolyzed keratin is added to conditioners and repair products so small keratin fragments smooth and strengthen damaged hair for a healthier, shinier look. A registered trial of a keratin peptide powder has no posted results.

lead: Hydrolyzed keratin is keratin, the structural protein of hair, wool, nails and feathers, that has been broken down into smaller peptide and amino-acid fragments so that it can dissolve in water. It is used as a protein ingredient in hair conditioners, masks and similar products, where it is marketed to make damaged hair look smoother, stronger and shinier.[1]

The appearance logic is that hair fibres cannot repair themselves, so conditioners work by coating the cuticle and filling gaps; small hydrolysed proteins are meant to deposit on or enter damaged strands, which gives a temporary improvement in smoothness and strength until shampooing removes the excess.[2] Native keratin is highly insoluble, largely because of disulfide bonds formed by the amino acid cysteine, and only certain reducing or dissolving agents can break it down. Hydrolyzed forms are made from sources such as feathers and wool and have also been studied as biomaterials for tissue engineering, films and nanofibres.[3][4]

Research on hair is mostly laboratory work. A 2025 study found that wool-derived hydrolyzed keratin deposits on the hair cuticle, partly penetrates the cortex and helped hair keep its tensile strength after UV exposure.[1] A registered trial of a hydrolyzed keratin peptide powder for hair health has been completed, but its results are not described in the registry record.[5]
infobox: Cysteine disulfide cross-links broken to give soluble peptides

paras: Keratin makes up hair, wool, nails, feathers and the outer layer of skin. Its toughness and insolubility come from cysteine-rich disulfide cross-links. Hydrolysis cleaves the protein chain into fragments small enough to be mixed into water-based formulas.
Besides cosmetics, hydrolyzed keratin has appeared in laboratory work on electrospun scaffolds, biodegradable plastic blends, cross-linked films and flocculants.[3][4][6][7]

Hydrolysis can be done chemically, enzymatically or with heat, and the resulting peptide size matters: one study summarised on Wikipedia found smaller keratin peptides penetrate deep into hair while larger fragments mostly stay on the surface.[2] Because the protein is rich in sulfur, hydrolysed keratin from chicken feathers has also been explored as a sulfur source for protein films.

Manufacturers add hydrolyzed keratin to conditioners and treatments with claims of smoothing, strengthening and repairing damaged strands. Hair conditioners in general reduce friction between strands and, according to Wikipedia, can neutralise the negative surface charge of weathered hair with cationic compounds; hydrolysed proteins are used to strengthen damaged hair, and the effect is temporary because shampooing removes the excess.[2]

The ingredient is also associated with keratin-based smoothing treatments, covered separately under keratin straightening. A 2025 laboratory study argues that wool-derived hydrolyzed keratin forms a film on the cuticle that acts as a UV reducer, and that under UV exposure it breaks down into smaller peptides and amino acids that can enter the hair interior.[1]

A registered trial (NCT07458828, started January 2024, 120 participants, completed) evaluated the efficacy and safety of a hydrolyzed keratin peptide powder on hair damage, hair health and hair strength; the registry entry lists no published results.[5]

A 2025 laboratory study used scanning electron microscopy and fluorescence penetration experiments on hair. It reported that hydrolyzed keratin formed a film on the cuticle and partly penetrated the cortex, and that tensile strength was maintained after UV exposure while untreated hair lost 14.32 percent.[1]

A 2026 study in the Journal of Medicinal Food examined orally administered hydrolyzed keratin peptide in male and female mice and its effect on human hair follicle dermal papilla cells and keratinocytes in culture; it is animal and cell research rather than a human trial.[8]

Other human work involves a randomized pilot study of 30 patients with knee osteoarthritis who took an oral supplement combining hydrolyzed collagen type II, chondroitin sulfate, hyaluronic acid and hydrolyzed keratin peptides for 4 weeks; the treated group showed improvement in WOMAC, Lequesne and pain scores, which is unrelated to appearance.[9] Most remaining literature is laboratory research on biomaterials.

Hydrolyzed keratin is a common label ingredient in salon-style repair conditioners and in the range of products that accompany keratin smoothing treatments. Conditioners trace back to natural-oil hair dressings such as Macassar oil in the 1800s, with silicones, fatty alcohols and protein ingredients added later.[2]
